newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech economy fundamentally sound - EU's Brittan.
newsitem.headline: Czech economy fundamentally sound - EU's Brittan.

text.p: The Czech economy is still fundamentally sound and the government is on the right track despite some recent problems, European External Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan said.

"The judgment of the European Union (EU) is that, of course, every country has its problems, but the progress the Czech economy has made has been remarkable and it remains fundamentally sound," Brittan said after meeting Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus.
The Czech Republic is seen as a leading contender to be among the first new members of the EU.
The Czech economy has enjoyed several years of consumption-led growth but the expansion has slowed recently.

Klaus told business leaders last week that the economy's biggest problem was its trade deficit, which widened to 160.3 billion crowns ($5.5 billion) in 1996 compared to 95.7 billion crowns ($3.3 billion) in the previous year.
"It is natural that there would be some trade imbalances at this stage of the development," Brittan told reporters.

But he praised the Czech government and said it was "investing heavily in the future". "The policies that are being followed are ones that led to great growth and will continue to do so in a stable way," he said.

Klaus has complained that the trade deficit with the EU, which grew to 125 billion crowns ($4.3 billion) in 1996 from 59.2 billion crowns ($2.03 billion) the previous year, was partly due to trade barriers preventing Czech goods reaching EU markets.
He told the business leaders gross domestic product (GDP) growth in 1996 was one percent lower than expected. Year-on-year GDP for third quarter 1996 was 3.6 percent.
The forecast for 1997 GDP growth has also been revised down to four percent from the 5.4 percent on which the budget was based, Klaus said.
